name: Robert Ross
bio: Canadian-born literary journalist, art critic and gallery-owner, grandson of Robert Baldwin, first Prime Minister of Upper Canada; brought to England aged two, he went up to King's College, Cambridge, in October 1888 and left abruptly in 1889 after a student-magazine libel, a ducking in the college fountain and a nervous breakdown. He met Wilde in 1886 and lodged with the Wildes at 16 Tite Street through part of 1887; he remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. In 1893 he and Lord Alfred Douglas were jointly threatened with prosecution over a schoolboy pupil of the Rev. Biscoe Wortham's at Bruges, and Ross spent the following winter out of reach at Davos. By 1897 he shared lodgings with More Adey at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington - by his biographer's account 'not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends' - and later ran the Carfax picture gallery with him. He kept daily attendance through Wilde's final illness, brought the priest who received Wilde into the Catholic Church, was at the bedside at the death on 30 November 1900, hired the Bagneux grave in his own name and moved the remains to Pere Lachaise in 1909. From early 1903 until the autumn of 1913 his life was shared with Frederick 'Freddie' Smith, a clerk of eighteen when they met, whom he employed as his secretary and with whom he openly set up house at 15 Vicarage Gardens, Kensington, from 1906. He published Wilde's De Profundis in 1905, cleared the estate of bankruptcy, became art critic and then art editor of the Morning Post, and was passed over for the directorship of the Tate. From 1911 Douglas and T. W. H. Crosland ran a campaign of surveillance and criminal accusation against him that produced the 1913 Ransome libel trial, Ross's own eight-day prosecution of Douglas at the Old Bailey, and the 1914 conspiracy proceedings; he was cleared, and afterwards lived quietly in rooms at 40 Half Moon Street, mentoring younger writers including Siegfried Sassoon and, through Sassoon, Wilfred Owen. He died there of heart failure on 5 October 1918, aged forty-nine.
bio_note: Born/died, Canadian origin, Baldwin descent, Cambridge dates, 1886 meeting, 'most faithful friend' and executorship from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 360 n. 1 (citing Margery Ross, Robert Ross: Friend of Friends, 1952, and Maureen Borland, Wilde's Devoted Friend, 1990). Hornton Street lodgings shared with Adey from the editorial note at p. 781 n. 2; Carfax partnership from p. 577 n. 2. Final illness, priest, deathbed and 'the grave is at Bagneux, in a temporary concession hired in my name' from Ross to More Adey, 14 Dec. 1900, Epilogue pp. 1219-1222; the 1909 removal to Père Lachaise from the editorial matter at p. 1230. From Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross: Oscar Wilde's Devoted Friend (2000): Cambridge arrival and abrupt departure, the ducking and breakdown: printed pp. 26-27, 33-35, 38-39. 1886 meeting and the 1887 Tite Street lodging: pp. 18, 21. Dansey/Bruges near-prosecution and Davos: pp. 78-81, 84, 237. Hornton Street with Adey and the 'not as lovers' formula: p. 66. Freddie Smith - meeting early 1903, ages, the secretaryship as cover: p. 177; move to 15 Vicarage Gardens: p. 192; 'his lover': p. 193; still flourishing at Lower Grosvenor Gardens: p. 214; ended autumn 1913: p. 230. Douglas's plea of justification and the Old Bailey trial from 19 November 1914: pp. 237-238. Half Moon Street from early summer 1914 and judgement in Ross's favour with costs: p. 243. Death on 5 October 1918 'aged just forty-nine' of heart failure: p. 258. Morning Post art editorship and the Tate directorship: index at printed pp. 199, 212-14, 251.
